big_idea: Complementary events: when ONE happens the OTHER doesn't. Heads OR tails. Rain OR no rain.
learning_intention: We are learning to name complementary events.
success_criteria: I can NAME a complementary event.
I can MATCH event-pairs that are complementary.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Lucky and Mae — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.

minds_on.hook: Mae: HEADS or TAILS! RAIN or NO RAIN! Either THIS happens or THAT happens — they're COMPLEMENTARY! Mae opens: 'EVENT — and its OPPOSITE! Both are POSSIBLE!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Lucky and Mae puppets. 'Friends — yesterday we reviewed likelihood. Today we learn COMPLEMENTARY events.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write COMPLEMENTARY EVENT on chart. 'Complementary = two events. When ONE happens, the OTHER doesn't.'

Demo. Show coin. 'HEADS or TAILS. If heads, NOT tails. If tails, NOT heads. They're complementary.'

More examples:
- Rain or no rain (Canadian weather).
- Win or lose (hockey game).
- Sunny or not sunny.
- Pass or fail (test).
- Day or night.
- Even or odd number on dice.

'Mae says — complementary events are EITHER-OR pairs. They CANNOT both happen at once.'

Non-example. 'Hot or cold' — could be WARM (in between). Not strictly complementary.

'Today we MATCH complementary events.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: match 4 events to their complements.
Three stations. A: Match 6 complement cards. B: Sort: complementary or not. C: Make own complement pair.
Stretch at C: 3 different complement pairs.
Discuss why 'hot or cold' is NOT strictly complementary.

STRATEGY COMPARE: 2-3 child-generated pairs to the carpet. Class votes 'complement or not?' and justifies. Cite Konold (1989) outcome-orientation — true complements partition all outcomes; partial complements miss the gap.
steps.teacher_prompt: Mae: 'A real complement leaves NO GAPS. Together they cover everything that could happen.'

differentiation.for_movement_learners: Children pair up; each pair is 'complementary' (one stands, one sits).

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: names complement; matches pairs; uses either-or.

consolidation.exit_routine: Mae's complement refrain — Mae calls 'EVENT — and its OPPOSITE!' Class: 'Both are POSSIBLE!' (3x). Each child writes one event and its complement on a sticky.

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 2 captures D2.1 mastery for complements.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child gives a NON-COMPLEMENT — repairing the not-strictly-complementary trap at Grade 2
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On complementary events, the trap is the outcome-orientation phenomenon (Konold 1989, 'Informal Conceptions of Probability'): child can name what happens but struggles to articulate the complement (what DOESN'T happen) as also a probability event. Jones, Langrall, Thornton & Mogill (1997) Level-2 transition frames this as the move from listing outcomes to relating them.

Yesterday Lucky reviewed likelihood. Today Mae introduces complementary events — 'rains' / 'doesn't rain' as a paired set. Lesson 3 spinners; Lesson 4 dice; Lesson 5 capstone.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair at Station C. Child writes 'hot or cold' as a complement pair.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'You wrote hot or cold. But Mae asks — could it be WARM? Yes! Warm is in between. So it's NOT strictly complementary.'

Guide. 'Strict complement: ONLY 2 outcomes. Heads or tails — no in-between. Rain or NO RAIN — either it rains or doesn't.'

Now practice. 'Even or odd — yes! Win or lose — yes (no tie counted). Sunny or not sunny — yes!'

If still confused: provide a checklist. 'Is there an in-between? If yes — not complementary.'
common_misconceptions: Any pair = complement. (Repair: complement = no in-between.)
Opposites = complement. (Repair: only if no third option.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child names event but not complement: drill 'what is the OPPOSITE outcome?' for 5 paired events; child says both before moving on.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child gives partial complement (e.g., 'it rains' / 'sunny' — but cloudy also exists): force binary framing 'rain OR no-rain'; child collapses to two outcomes.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child can name complement but doesn't see it as a probability event: ask 'is the complement possible? certain? impossible?' Child re-categorises both.

parts_outline.task: Write 3 of your own complement pairs.
